claim: Remark 5.3 of Bitar--Donoso--Petite, arXiv:2609.26479v1, is false for the paper's stated notion of strong double minimality unless an effectiveness hypothesis is added. Let \(G=\mathbb Z\times S_3\) and let \(\pi:G\to\mathbb Z\) be projection. Since \(Z(S_3)=\{e\}\), one has \(Z(G)=\mathbb Z\times\{e\}\) and hence \(\pi(Z(G))=\mathbb Z=Z(\mathbb Z)\). Take any strong doubly minimal \(\mathbb Z\)-system and pull it back along \(\pi\). Proposition 5.15 of the same paper proves that this pullback is again strong doubly minimal, while every element of \(\ker\pi\) acts trivially. But \(g=(0,(12))\) is noncentral and has finite conjugacy class, so \(g\in\operatorname{FC}(G)\setminus Z(G)\). Thus \(G\) admits a strong doubly minimal action despite \(\operatorname{FC}(G)\setminus Z(G)\ne\varnothing\), contradicting the group-level conclusion of Remark 5.3. The proof in Remark 5.3 fails here because the graph of \(S^g=\operatorname{id}\) is the diagonal, and Definition 5.1 imposes density only on pairs from different \(Z(G)\)-orbits. No claim is made against a faithful or effective-action version of the obstruction.

correctness.rationale: The group computation is exact: \(Z(S_3)=\{e\}\), hence \(Z(\mathbb Z\times S_3)=\mathbb Z\times\{e\}\), and projection to \(\mathbb Z\) maps the center onto the center. Proposition 5.15 therefore produces a strong doubly minimal pullback from any classical strong doubly minimal \(\mathbb Z\)-system. The element \((0,(12))\) is noncentral and has a three-element conjugacy class, placing it in \(\operatorname{FC}(G)\setminus Z(G)\). Because it lies in the kernel, its action is the identity and its graph is the diagonal; Definition 5.1 excludes same-central-orbit pairs from the density requirement. This is a direct contradiction to Remark 5.3 as stated, with no experimental step.

value.rationale: The finding exposes a structural incompatibility inside a recent paper's theory: a stated obstruction on the acting group is defeated by the paper's own general pullback construction. The explicit \(\mathbb Z\times S_3\) example shows exactly why nonfaithful kernel elements make the finite-orbit graph harmless under Definition 5.1. This is mathematically useful because it identifies an effectiveness issue that must be handled whenever sTMSJ is transported between groups, while leaving unrelated main results untouched.
